newsitem.title: INDIA: India stocks levelling off, more gains in 98 - SocGen.
newsitem.headline: India stocks levelling off, more gains in 98 - SocGen.

text.p: India's booming stock markets may have neared a plateau, but are likely add another 20 percent to values in a year's time, Sanjeev Sanyal, economist at Soc-Gen Crosby India, said on Wednesday.
"At this point we think that the market is ... almost fully valued," Sanjeev Sanyal, economist at Soc-Gen Crosby India, told Reuters Financial Television.
"So, we don't think the market in itself will rise too much further," he said.
However, he saw the market going up in the longer term.
"Looking at it in a one-year perspective we see probably a 20 percent uptrend from these levels," he said.
In the short run political instability concerns would keep the markets from rising too sharply from current levels over the next three months, he said.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark 30-share index ended 35.38 points, or 0.84 percent, lower at a provsiional 4,185.64 -- after hitting a 33-month high of 4,448.06 last week -- largely due to a correction set off by a partner's threat to withdraw from India's minority coalition government.
Sanyal said foreign inflows were a crucial factor in India's stocks boom.
"Clearly, there's a problem with the rest of Asia. So, to some extent there's a safe-haven factor," he said.
Other factors like expectations of economic revival, falling interest rates and abundant liquidity also aided the upswing.

"We expect that in the next 3-4 months definite signs of revival would come through," he said, adding that global and domestic liquidity, low interest rates and rising money supply would feed the recovery.
He said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is likely to cap a strong rupee and allow money supply to rise.
"Probably they (the RBI) will have money supply growth .. rather than allow the rupee to rise because export markets have been quite sluggish and they are concerned about that," he said.
"We do not expect the rupee to appreciate too much but definitely remain at this level," he said.
The rupee ended at near seven-month highs of 35.70 to a dollar on Wednesday despite the central bank's intravention to stall the rupee's rise.

He said the central bank had been fighting a battle on two fronts -- by buying up rising dollar inflows to keep the rupee from appreciating, and controlling domestic money supply growth by heavy borrowings.
The RBI has already raised nearly 60 percent of the borrowings programme for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March), and it would reach its target by September, he said.
"It will find that it will either have to let the currency appreciate or it will have to allow money supply to rise very sharply," Sanyal said.
The Indian economy which was suffering from a demand problem and huge overcapacity may come to the RBI's rescue, he said.
"They might feel that excess money supply will feed into production rather than inflation," he said. "So, given the choice that might be the best option."

Sanyal said the upward pressure on the rupee would continue for at least seven months because of planned government plans to divest holdings in state-run firms through global depositary receipts issues.
One such issue by Gas Authority of India Ltd would alone bring in about $800 million, he said.
Over the longer term the rupee would depreciate, he said.
"Looking further out I think the rupee in real exchange rate terms is about 7-8 percent overvalued," he said.
"In the longer run it will probably have to depreciate keeping in mind that all its competitors are depreciating at this moment of time in South Asia," he added. an economist said on Wednesday.
